title: Wages Owed and a Brother's Wedding
scenario: Rohan Das, 28, works construction in Doha and sends most of his pay to his family in Sylhet. His employer is three months behind on wages, and Rohan's brother is marrying next month, with the family expecting Rohan to cover the feast. A recruitment agent offers a short-term loan at high interest. Rohan fears complaining could cost him his visa. He must decide this week how to answer his family.
options: Take the high-interest loan and send money for the wedding, preserving family honour at the risk of deepening his debt.
Tell his family honestly that he cannot send money now, accepting their disappointment and the damage to his standing.
File a complaint with the labour authority and ask the family to scale back, risking his job and visa for a chance to recover wages.

title: The Au Pair's Second Family
scenario: Mariana Vlad, 24, from Moldova, works as a live-in nanny in Vienna for a family she has come to love. Her mother back home has asked her to return and care for her younger brothers after their father left. Meanwhile, her employers have offered Mariana help with a work permit for a long-term stay. Her wages support the entire household in Chisinau. Mariana must give her employers an answer by the end of the week.
options: Return to Moldova to care for her brothers, accepting a drop in income and the loss of the opportunity in Vienna.
Stay in Vienna with the work permit and keep sending money, hiring a relative to help care for the boys.
Stay for another year to build savings and bring her brothers over later, delaying the family's immediate needs.

title: Remitting to the Wrong Brother
scenario: Ifeoma Nwosu, a 37-year-old nurse in Houston, sends monthly money to her family in Enugu, intended for her mother's care. She learns that her brother Chukwudi, who receives the transfer, has been spending part on a failing business. Her mother has never complained. Confronting Chukwudi could cause a break, and sending money elsewhere would shame him. Ifeoma must decide how to handle the next transfer, due in three days.
options: Confront Chukwudi directly and set conditions on the money, treating her mother's care as the priority.
Send the money to a different relative or directly to the mother, bypassing Chukwudi without an explanation to protect the peace.
Keep sending to Chukwudi and give additional funds to her mother in person during a visit, avoiding confrontation.

title: A Visa for One
scenario: Habib Rahmani, 33, a Syrian engineer, has been resettled in Hamburg. He is entitled to bring his wife and one child; his elderly parents and a teenage sister remain in a camp near Gaziantep. Family reunification rules allow him to apply only for his wife and daughter first. His father, proud and unwell, says the parents will manage. Habib's sister would be left alone with them. He must decide whom to include on the application.
options: Apply for his wife and daughter first as the rules suggest, trusting that his parents will survive until a later application.
Delay the application to prepare a case for the sister's inclusion, risking his wife and daughter's safety in the interim.
Apply for his wife and sister, leaving his daughter with the grandparents temporarily, a painful separation he thinks may be necessary.

title: Sacrificing the Scholarship
scenario: Sanele Khumalo, 20, from a village in KwaZulu-Natal, has won a scholarship to study engineering in Cape Town. His father, a miner, has been laid off, and his younger sisters' school fees are due. An uncle in Johannesburg offers Sanele a job in a warehouse with wages he could send home. The scholarship deadline to accept is in a week. Sanele's mother says she will never ask him to give up studying. He must decide.
options: Accept the scholarship and trust that his sisters' fees can be found through other means, treating education as the best long-term help.
Take the job in Johannesburg and defer the scholarship, ensuring immediate support for his sisters.
Accept the scholarship and seek part-time work in Cape Town, sending a little money but accepting heavy strain on his studies.

title: The Mother Who Wasn't Told
scenario: Prakriti Sharma, a 31-year-old Nepali kitchen worker in Kuala Lumpur, has been dismissed after an injury and has not told her mother, who relies on her remittances and has been boasting about her daughter's good job. Prakriti has a little savings that would last two months. A broker offers her a place on a farm job in Malaysia's interior at a lower wage with a hefty placement fee. She must decide how to handle the next call from home.
options: Tell her mother the truth and ask the family to adjust, accepting shame but ending the deception.
Take the farm job and keep sending reduced amounts without explaining, preserving her mother's pride.
Use her savings to keep sending the usual amount for two months while searching for work, delaying the truth.

title: Left Behind with Grandmother
scenario: Teresa Gomes, 34, a care assistant in Lisbon from Cape Verde, left her nine-year-old son Dinis with his grandmother in Praia when she migrated. For six years she has sent money and visited in summers. Dinis now says he doesn't see her as his mother. A chance has arisen to bring him to Portugal, but his grandmother is distressed at losing him, and Dinis is happy in school. Teresa must say what she wants during her next call.
options: Bring Dinis to Lisbon, asserting her place as his mother and the importance of being together as a family.
Leave Dinis with his grandmother for now and visit more often, prioritising his current stability and relationships.
Ask Dinis what he wants and let that guide the decision, though a nine-year-old may not grasp the long-term stakes.

title: The Savings Group Treasurer
scenario: Mwajuma Said, 45, treasurer of a Tanzanian diaspora savings circle in Muscat, discovers that a member, Halima, has lost her job and cannot contribute. The circle's rules demand expulsion after three missed payments, and others have their own tight budgets. Halima's family back home depends on her. Expelling her would take away her share just when she needs it. Mwajuma must decide whether to propose enforcing the rule at the next gathering.
options: Enforce the rule as written, treating consistent rules as the basis of the group's trust and fairness to all members.
Propose a temporary suspension of Halima's payments and absorb the cost across the group, prioritising her need.
Offer Halima a personal loan from Mwajuma's own funds in secret so the circle's rules remain unchanged.
tension: fairness to members vs. member in need

title: A Family Home Built on Absence
scenario: For twelve years, Jorge Ayala, 52, has worked as a landscaper in Madrid, sending money to build a large house in Cuenca, Ecuador, where he planned to retire. His wife, Lucia, who stayed behind, has recently told him she has begun a relationship with someone else and wants the house in her name. His teenage children live with her. Jorge must decide whether to return to Ecuador to fight for the house and his children or remain in Spain.
options: Return to Ecuador to contest the house and be with his children, accepting loss of income and the end of his Spanish life.
Remain in Spain and negotiate through a lawyer, prioritising his earnings and avoiding a bitter confrontation.
Agree to put the house in the children's names and remain abroad, protecting their security while ending the dispute.

title: Payment for a Cousin's Crossing
scenario: Mehmet Aydin, 38, a taxi driver in Cologne, receives a call from his cousin Bilal in Izmir, desperate to leave Turkey and asking Mehmet to lend him money for a smuggler. Mehmet knows such crossings can be deadly. Bilal says that without Mehmet he will use less safe means. Mehmet has savings but also family obligations in Germany. Mehmet's mother says family comes first and implies he should help. He must decide what to say to Bilal tonight.
options: Lend Bilal the money, reasoning that Bilal will go anyway and a safer route is better than none.
Refuse to fund the crossing and instead offer help seeking legal visas or work routes, even if slower and less likely to succeed.
Refuse and try to dissuade Bilal, even at the cost of the relationship, believing the risk of death is too high.
tension: family loyalty vs. risk to life

title: The Coconut Farm and the Cruise Ship
scenario: Ricardo Santos, 25, works on a cruise ship, sending his wages to his parents in Cebu to hire farm workers. His father is aging and wants Ricardo to come home and manage the coconut farm. Ricardo's contract will end in four months, and a renewal would pay double what farming yields. His fiancee wants to settle near her family in Manila. His father says the land will be lost if Ricardo does not return. He must decide whether to renew.
options: Renew his contract and send more money, hiring a manager for the farm and prioritising income.
Return home to manage the farm, honouring his father's wish and the land at the cost of earnings.
Return briefly to train a relative as manager and then go back to sea, trying to hold both responsibilities.

title: Rent Money or Funeral Money
scenario: Aliou Camara, 41, a street vendor in Marseille from Guinea, has saved enough for rent for three months. His brother in Conakry dies suddenly, and the family asks Aliou to fund the funeral and bring his body home, a cost equal to nearly six months' rent. Failing to do so would bring deep shame. If he uses the money, he may face eviction. Aliou has a day to reply to his family.
options: Pay for the funeral in full, honouring his brother and family and risking eviction in France.
Fund a simpler burial in France with a ceremony back home, saving money but facing criticism for not bringing the body home.
Send part of the cost and ask relatives to contribute the rest, accepting reputational cost and hoping for community support.

title: A Debt to the Village Elders
scenario: Pema Lhamo, 29, a hotel worker in Delhi from Ladakh, learns that the village elders paid for her mother's medical treatment on the understanding that Pema would send money for a communal prayer hall renovation. Pema has been laid off in the city and has little to give. The elders say the debt is one of honour. Pema's mother says she is not asking Pema to bankrupt herself. Pema must reply to the village council in a letter.
options: Pay what she can in installments and be honest about her situation, acknowledging the debt while setting limits.
Tell the council she cannot pay anything now and ask for forgiveness, risking disgrace and her mother's standing.
Borrow money from a friend in Delhi to pay in full, preserving honour at the price of new personal debt.

title: What the Remittance Platform Knows
scenario: Hye-jin Oh, a compliance analyst at a money-transfer company in Seoul, notices that a migrant worker, Nguyen, is sending small repeated transfers to an account in Hanoi that matches a pattern flagged for possible money laundering. She suspects instead that he is funding relatives through multiple recipients to avoid fees. Reporting would freeze his account for weeks, harming his family. Staying silent could violate her duty. Hye-jin must decide today whether to file the report.
options: File the report as the compliance policy requires, accepting the harm to a probably innocent family.
Escalate to her manager with a note that the pattern likely has an innocent explanation, delaying the freeze while following process.
Quietly mark it as reviewed and take no action, trusting her own judgement over the policy but risking her job.

title: The Interpreter at the Clinic
scenario: Fatima Hussein, 40, from Somalia, living in Minneapolis, is asked by her cousin's family in Mogadishu to send money for emergency surgery for a child. At the same time her own daughter's school is asking for a fee for a trip. Her husband says their savings must go toward a house deposit as agreed. Fatima knows the cousin's child may die without surgery. She must tell her husband tonight what she wants to do with their savings.
options: Send the money for surgery and delay the house deposit, treating a child's life as the overriding need.
Send a partial amount and ask the wider clan to cover the rest, balancing obligations without full sacrifice.
Keep the savings for the house deposit and send only a small gift, putting the immediate family's long-term security first.
tension: life of a relative vs. household security

title: Return of the Prodigal Engineer
scenario: After eighteen years in Toronto, Obinna Eze, 49, an engineer from Nigeria, is offered a government infrastructure role in Abuja. His parents pressure him to return and help rebuild the country. His teenage children, born in Canada, protest they do not want to move, and his wife has a career. The job pays a third of his current salary. Obinna must give the government his answer before the end of the month.
options: Take the role and move the family, believing in contributing to his homeland and the example to his children.
Decline and keep sending support, preserving his children's stability and family finances.
Take the role alone for two years while the family remains in Canada, risking the strain of long separation.

title: Cutting Off the Cousin
scenario: Dmytro Kovalenko, 36, who works in a warehouse in Prague after fleeing Ukraine, has sent money regularly to his sister in Kharkiv. He learns that his cousin Oleh, who lives with her, has been drinking and taking the money. His sister says she needs Oleh to stay for safety and company. Dmytro could stop sending funds, cutting off Oleh but also making his sister's life harder, or insist that Oleh leaves. He must decide what to say during tonight's call.
options: Demand that Oleh leave and threaten to stop remittances, prioritising his sister's welfare over her stated wish.
Continue sending money and trust his sister's judgement, respecting her autonomy and the realities of war.
Change how he sends money, paying landlord and grocery bills directly so Oleh cannot divert it, without confronting anyone.

title: Sponsored Sister, Unreliable Promise
scenario: Leila Mansour, 43, a Lebanese-Canadian dentist in Montreal, has signed to sponsor her cousin Rima's immigration, which commits her financially for Rima for ten years. Rima arrives and soon moves out, stops answering Leila's calls, and is rumoured to have taken cash work. Leila is held liable by authorities for Rima's use of public benefits. Her husband says she should report Rima to limit liability. Leila must decide what to do.
options: Report Rima's situation to the authorities to limit her liability, prioritising her household's finances and legal obligations.
Stay silent and accept the liability, honouring the cousin relationship and hoping Rima will be reconciled.
Try again to reach Rima and lay out the risks to both of them before taking any official step.

title: The Seasonal Orchard Contract
scenario: Anita Bhandari, a 30-year-old Nepali worker, is offered a fruit-picking season in New Zealand under a scheme that requires leaving her six-year-old behind with her sister for nine months. Her husband, a driver, is out of work and the family has debts. A neighbour who went last year says the work is hard but fair. Her child has asthma and relies on Anita's care. Anita must tell the recruiter by tomorrow.
options: Accept the contract, trusting the sister to care for the child and viewing the income as vital to family security.
Decline, prioritising her sick child's daily care and accepting continued debts and financial hardship.
Ask her husband to take the contract instead, though it would be harder for him to be accepted and she would carry the debt.

title: Speaking for Parents in a New Land
scenario: Delia Constantin, 17, in Dublin, has translated for her Romanian parents since arriving three years ago. Her parents' employer is cutting hours and has sent a letter that Delia reads as hinting at a pretext to dismiss them without proper notice. Her parents say not to cause trouble, because they need the work to send money back to relatives. Delia's teacher, Mr. Fahey, notices her stress and offers to connect them with an advice service. Delia must decide whether to ask for it.
options: Accept the help and show the letter to the advice service, believing her parents' rights matter more than their fear.
Decline the help and follow her parents' wishes, preserving their sense of control and avoiding risk of retaliation.
Ask the service for general information without naming the employer, and decide with her parents afterward.

title: One Passport for Four Siblings
scenario: Amara Okeke's family in Port Harcourt has saved to send one child abroad, hoping to bring the rest later. Four siblings have applied for a student visa pathway in Canada, with only enough funds for one. Amara, 26, the eldest and a competent but average student, is expected to decide. Her youngest brother Emeka has the best grades but is only 17. Amara can send herself, with a job to follow, or send Emeka, who would need years of support. She must make the proposal to her parents.
options: Send herself, since she is older and likelier to find work quickly and send money back to the others.
Send Emeka, whose long-term prospects are strongest, even though it delays support and uses her sacrifice.
Send the sibling who gets the best offer from a school after all applications are decided, delaying a choice but removing her personal decision.

title: Returning a Lost Wallet
scenario: Stefan Petrov, 31, a Bulgarian dishwasher in Brussels, finds an envelope with the equivalent of two months' pay near the restaurant's back door. The restaurant owner lost it, he suspects, but no one has asked. His mother in Plovdiv urgently needs a dental operation and his savings are short. Stefan could return the envelope with honest embarrassment, or tell himself it was found money. He must decide before the owner returns tomorrow morning.
options: Return it unopened, valuing honesty and his own integrity regardless of his family's need.
Keep the money and send it to his mother, reasoning that her immediate suffering outweighs a loss the owner can absorb.
Return it and ask the owner for a loan or advance, risking a no but acting honestly while seeking help.

title: A Pension Sent Across the Strait
scenario: Wen-Hsin Tsai, 63, retired from a Taiwanese electronics company, receives a decent pension. Her sister in Fujian, who cared for their parents for decades, is now ill and asks for large monthly sums. Taiwan's rules on cross-strait transfers are complicated, and her own children say Wen-Hsin should save for her own old age. Wen-Hsin feels she owes her sister for years of care. She must decide how much to commit to sending.
options: Send the large monthly sums her sister needs, treating the debt of care as binding and her own children's concerns as secondary.
Send a smaller fixed amount, balancing obligation to her sister and her own security.
Pay for a single major medical procedure and explain she cannot continue, concentrating help where it matters most.

title: Money Orders and a Gambling Son
scenario: Rosa Cabrera, 57, a hotel cleaner in Los Angeles from Guatemala, sends her son Elias, 24, rent money each month in Quetzaltenango. A friend there reports that Elias bets on online games and rarely works. Rosa's husband died years ago and Elias is her only child. Rosa fears that cutting him off would push him toward worse things and that he would resent her. She also needs savings for her own retirement. She must decide how to handle the next transfer.
options: Stop sending money until Elias finds work, accepting the pain and risk to hold him accountable.
Keep sending rent but pay the landlord directly, ensuring housing while limiting what can be used for gambling.
Visit Guatemala to see for herself before deciding, spending money and time on a trip she can barely afford.

title: Dual Citizenship and a Draft Notice
scenario: Andrei Popescu, 22, a Romanian-Israeli student in Cluj, receives a notice from Israeli authorities that he is due to report for military service at home. His mother, who immigrated years earlier, wants him to serve for the sake of family ties and honour; his father back in Romania wants him to stay and avoid danger. Andrei is unsure about the politics and fears for his safety. Andrei must write his answer to the consulate by the deadline.
options: Report for service, honouring his mother's wishes and the duty he feels from his dual citizenship.
Decline to report, accepting that he may be barred from returning and valuing his own safety and conscience.
Request a deferment for study, trying to delay without fully refusing, though it may only postpone the decision.
tension: obligation to a second homeland vs. personal safety
